title: Downhill Running: What Are The Effects and How Can We Adapt? A Narrative Review
authors: Bontemps B, Vercruyssen F, Gruet M, Louis J
population: Studies of downhill running protocols; populations and protocols differ between studies
findings: Downhill running can reduce performance by exercise-induced muscle damage, mostly measured by isometric MVC, creatine kinase and soreness.
Slope, duration and speed are the main influencing factors; the median protocol used was -12% slope (Q1-Q3 -15% to -10%), 40 min (30-45 min) and 11.3 km/h (9.8-12.9 km/h).
People least accustomed to downhill running generally showed the most muscle damage.
Prior downhill exposure is the most effective preventive strategy found.
Compression garments and special footwear were unconfirmed.
Protocols and outcome measures varied widely between studies, preventing firm conclusions on moderators.
limitations: Narrative review with no quantitative synthesis. The abstract states that discrepancies in assessing damage, protocols and populations prevent firm conclusions.
implications: Introduce downhill running progressively and place the first exposure well ahead of a race with large descents, since prior exposure is the best-supported preventive strategy and the least accustomed show the most damage.

Treat an unaccustomed downhill session near the typical research protocol (median -12% slope, 40 min, 11.3 km/h; Q1-Q3 -15% to -10%, 30-45 min, 9.8-12.9 km/h) as high-damage load. A specific recovery window is not given in the abstract.
Do not rely on compression garments or special footwear as a plan element; their effectiveness is unconfirmed.

verification.notes: Crossref: Sports Medicine 50(12):2083-2110, 2020, four authors match. Europe PMC PMID 33037592 abstract supports all numbers. Removed the unsupported 'mostly young adults' claim and the 48-72 h recovery number.
